scope: 1st Tank Corps / Yasuoka Detachment armored phase, late Jun-Jul 1939; broader Aug campaign unchanged pending later audit

operational: Japanese armored regiments were committed hurriedly and without adequate combined-arms integration.
US Army historical study describes both Japanese regiments as failing to break Soviet defenses and losing roughly half their armor operationally in the early July fighting.
By 9 July the 3rd Tank Regiment had only about a half-dozen operational tanks associated with its supply/maintenance company.
Japanese primary battle reports explicitly include casualty, weapons/ammunition-loss and fuel-loss appendices and describe wet-ground movement delays and support problems.

loss_series_guard.provisional_secondary_anchor: 42 Japanese tanks disabled, of which 29 were reportedly later repaired/redeployed; exact vehicle-class/regiment breakdown remains to be transcribed from primary appendices.
loss_series_guard.use: sensitivity anchor only, not promoted archival truth

branch_vehicle_change.scope: running gear, cooling/lubrication, tolerance consistency, recovery/repair organization; gun/armor unchanged
branch_vehicle_change.important: higher dispatchability increases exposure and combat contacts; it does not simply reduce all losses

first_pass_quantitative_effect.meaning: roughly 18-35% more useful armored combat-days before withdrawal/dissolution, not 18-35% more tanks surviving the war

Japanese_AFV_damaged_disabled.reason: more sorties/contact offsets improved mechanical reliability; total damaged can stay similar or rise

Japanese_AFV_irrecoverable.reason: better recovery/repair saves a few hulls, but Soviet 45mm/artillery kills and captured vehicles remain irreversible

operational_extension.armored_useful_presence: 2-4 additional days of credible local armored support before withdrawal becomes the rational decision
operational_extension.guard: not retained into the decisive August Soviet offensive; fuel/logistics/support and Soviet superiority still force withdrawal

Japanese_personnel.attached_infantry_engineer_artillery_KW_: roughly -90 to -190 K/W/M during the early-July armored phase
Japanese_personnel.mechanism: more suppression, covered withdrawal/recovery, fewer Soviet armored penetrations into exposed supporting troops
Japanese_personnel.not_claimed: No large reduction in the total Nomonhan catastrophe; the decisive Aug battles occur after armor withdrawal.

Japanese_other_equipment.reason: extra armored cover during local disengagement/recovery; very uncertain

Soviet_Mongolian_personnel.mechanism: additional firing cycles and local positions attacked before Japanese armor is withdrawn

Soviet_AFV.guard: not all are permanent losses; Soviet recovery capability is substantial

Japanese_consumption.recovery_engineer_commitment: higher, not lower, because more damaged vehicles are worth recovering

time_space.effect: some Soviet local attacks delayed by hours to about one day; Japanese withdrawals somewhat better covered
time_space.strategic_result: UNCHANGED: no Japanese breakthrough, armored detachment still dissolved/withdrawn, Nomonhan strategic defeat remains

institutional_effect.branch_lesson: Tanks are not dismissed as mechanically unreliable curiosities. The lesson becomes: armor is tactically valuable when serviceable, but under-gunned and crippled by poor combined-arms/logistics integration.
downstream: more emphasis on recovery, fuel, engineers, radio and tank-infantry-artillery coordination
no evidence for an immediate heavy-tank leap

confidence.next_primary_source_task: Transcribe 3rd/4th Tank Regiment loss appendices to replace the 42/29 secondary anchor and tighten crew/equipment effects.
